data.raw_text:
A Japanese Army officer raising a final toast of 'sake' (nihonshu) before departing for a one way no return mission toward Leyte in November 1944....

On the night of November 26, 1944, the Kaoru Airborne Raiding Detachment (Kaoru Koteitai/Kaoru Unit) departed from Lipa Airfield south of Manila on Luzon, Philippines, for a suicide (kamikaze) air-landing mission to Leyte. They boarded four Showa L2D2 "Tabby" twin-engined light transport aircraft (licensed Japanese versions of the American Douglas DC-3).

The Kaoru Koteitai was the 1st Guerrilla Company (1st Yugekitai), a specialized unit formed under the Japanese 4th Air Army. It was largely composed of Takasago ethnic group members from Formosa (Taiwan), who were recognized for their elite jungle-fighting skills. A total of 40 men participated in the mission, with 10 raiders assigned to each of the four aircraft. The mission, designated Operation Gi, was intended as a "kamikaze" style air-landing operation where the transports would deliberately make belly-landings on the North and South Burauen airfields on Leyte to allow the raiders to destroy parked American aircraft and installations.

The mission ended in total failure. Most, if not all, of the transport aircraft carrying the detachment were destroyed by American fire before or during landing attempts. The raid did not disrupt Allied operations on Leyte, which by late November was already heavily secured by American forces.

© History Pictures

#archaeohistories
